name.text: L2 Q1 Image and running machine

questiontext.text: What is the relationship between a machine image and a virtual machine?

generalfeedback.text: An image provides the starting state for multiple instances. The instances can change independently after launch; those changes do not automatically rewrite the image.

answer.text: The image is a live record of the machine's current CPU and memory usage.
Each image can start a single VM, so a second VM needs its own copy of the image.
When a running VM changes, those changes are usually written back to its source image.
One image can start many VMs, and each VM can then change independently.

name.text: L2 Q2 Image building and deployment

questiontext.text: What distinguishes building a machine image from deploying machines based on that image?

generalfeedback.text: Image building prepares a reusable artifact. Deployment uses that artifact to create running instances. Producing a new image does not automatically update existing machines or eliminate instance-specific initialization.

answer.text: Building creates a reusable artifact; deploying starts running machines from it.
Building a new image also updates the machines that were started from the old one.
Deploying a machine updates the shared source image whenever that machine changes.
Building an image removes the need for any instance-specific configuration at launch.

questiontext.text: A team calls its base server image the "golden image." Which property of that image would make it an anti-pattern?

generalfeedback.text: The problem is hidden manual changes and the lack of a maintained, repeatable creation process. A shared baseline or an automated, rebuildable image is not inherently an anti-pattern, even if the team calls it a golden image.

answer.text: The organization shares one base image across many teams and services.
The image is tested before use, which slows down releases.
It was changed by hand and cannot be rebuilt from a maintained definition.
The image is produced by an automated pipeline instead of by an administrator.

questiontext.text: A team wants to use the same machine baseline on two virtualization platforms and on different processor architectures. Which assumption is sound?

generalfeedback.text: Machine images must be compatible with the destination platform and processor architecture. A common intended baseline can require different artifacts or formats for different targets; the exact requirements depend on the target platforms.

answer.text: A machine image can usually boot unchanged on any platform and processor architecture.
Check each platform and architecture; you may need separate image variants.
If the application name and version match, the machine images will be compatible.
The disk size is what decides whether an image can boot on a platform.

name.text: L2 Q5 Stock and custom images

questiontext.text: An organization starts every server from a supplied stock image and repeats the same security and software setup at launch. What is the strongest reason to maintain a custom image?

generalfeedback.text: A stock image is a supplied starting point. A custom image adds selected software and configuration, providing a tested baseline and reducing repeated initialization. It still requires maintenance, instance-specific settings, and separate protection of persistent data.

answer.text: It provides a tested company baseline, which reduces repeated setup but still needs maintenance.
It captures live application data, so separate data backups are no longer needed.
It picks up future security fixes as they are released, so its build definition can stay unchanged.
It removes environment differences, so settings and machine identities should be built into it as well.

name.text: L2 Q6 Build time and boot time

questiontext.text: A fleet needs the same monitoring software on every machine, but each instance needs a distinct identity and environment-specific connection settings. Which division of work best fits image building and boot-time initialization?

generalfeedback.text: Build-time work becomes part of a reusable image; boot-time initialization can supply values specific to an instance or environment. Other divisions may be valid, but this one directly separates the stable shared baseline from the varying inputs. Boot-time initialization alone is not ongoing reconciliation.

answer.text: Put the monitoring software and one shared machine identity in the image; change environment settings by hand after launch.
Install everything at boot time, because a reusable image cannot contain configured software.
Put the monitoring software in the image; supply identity and environment settings during boot-time initialization.
Put the production connection settings in each image, and keep boot-time initialization for a check that the machine boots.

name.text: L2 Q7 Containers and virtual machines

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly compares a typical Linux container with a virtual machine and identifies a consequence?

generalfeedback.text: Typical Linux containers share a host kernel while isolating aspects of their execution environment. A VM has a guest kernel over virtualized hardware. Kernel sharing affects compatibility and isolation; neither approach guarantees that arbitrary images work on every platform.

answer.text: Containers and VMs both boot their own kernel, so they provide the same kernel isolation boundary.
Containers share the host kernel, so a process in one container can see and change files in another.
VMs run their own guest kernel, which means any VM image can run unchanged on every processor architecture and hypervisor.
Containers share the host kernel and VMs run their own, so a workload needing another kernel may need a VM.

name.text: L2 Q8 Snapshot and rebuildable definition

questiontext.text: A team has a snapshot of a working server but no maintained definition of how it was configured. Which assessment is most accurate?

generalfeedback.text: A snapshot captures state at a point in time, within its scope and consistency limits. It can support restoration but does not explain the intended build process or make hidden manual changes reviewable. Rebuildable definitions and data backups serve different purposes.

answer.text: It records how the server was configured, so future changes can be reviewed from its creation history.
It can restore the captured state, yet a maintained definition is needed to review and rebuild the setup.
It is of no use for recovery, because restoring a machine requires a rebuildable definition.
It shows that future builds will match the server, as long as the same stock image name is selected.

name.text: L2 Q9 Organizing an image family

questiontext.text: Web-server and database-server images share a security baseline but need different software. Their separate build definitions contain copied baseline steps, and a policy update reached only one copy. Which plan best addresses both organization and rollout?

generalfeedback.text: A shared baseline reduces inconsistent copies while workload-specific definitions preserve useful differences. Updating source does not update existing artifacts or instances: affected images must be rebuilt, tested, and deliberately rolled out. Validation should cover both the policy and the workloads.

answer.text: Build one image with both workloads installed, and apply baseline changes to whichever running servers currently need them.
Share a common baseline with separate workload definitions; committing a new baseline version also updates existing images and running machines.
Share a common baseline with separate workload definitions; rebuild affected images, test policy and workloads, then replace machines deliberately.
Keep the copied baseline steps and review each copy, then validate the baseline definition before replacing machines from existing images.

name.text: L2 Q10 Reproducible builds and immutable updates

questiontext.text: A version-controlled image build always selects the latest base image and packages. The team wants to reproduce an approved version and later roll out a deliberately patched version. Which plan meets both goals?

generalfeedback.text: Version-controlled instructions do not freeze external inputs such as base images and packages, so reproduction requires controlled versions and available artifacts. A built image is a versioned artifact: keeping the previous version allows a rollback, and each new image is tested before release. An immutable update builds and validates a new image, replaces instances deliberately, and protects persistent data through separate storage or a verified copy. Done this way, machines can be replaced in minutes while their data is preserved.

answer.text: Pin and keep the approved base image and packages; build and test a patched image, then replace instances while protecting persistent data.
Re-run the same source revision with the latest inputs, update existing servers in place, and call the unchanged source an immutable release.
Record the approved base image but keep selecting the latest packages, then replace the machines and rebuild their data from the build definition.
Control both base and package versions, patch running machines by hand, and rely on their original image for any future replacement.
